lead: Assembly programs rarely run straight through once. They repeat a block a fixed number of times, walk a pointer through memory, or waste exact time before the next hardware action. Counters and index registers make these loops; T-state counting turns a loop into a delay; a look-up table turns an index into a stored constant. You meet all three in keypad scanning, seven-segment displays, motor step timing and sensor linearisation.
prereq: You need: 3.5 for conditional jumps, 3.4 for DCR and the Z flag, and Unit 2 for T-states and machine cycles.

sections.h3: Loops with a counter or an index

blocks.text: A loop repeats a block until a test says stop. In assembly the test is usually a decrement followed by a conditional jump. A counter register holds the repeat count. DCR counter reduces it by one and sets the Z flag when the result is zero. JNZ jumps back while Z = 0. This is a count-down loop: the count runs from N to zero.

items: Load the counter with N, the number of passes.
Test Z: if Z = 0, jump back to the body; if Z = 1, fall through.
Reload the counter before starting a new loop.

blocks.text: An index register holds an address, not a count. Load the base address into HL. MOV A,M reads the byte at that address, and INX H moves to the next byte. Decrement the counter and jump back. The same pattern copies a block, sums an array, or sends a table of bytes to a port.

blocks.code:
LXI H, 2000H
MVI C, 05H
LOOP: MOV A,M
INX H
DCR C
JNZ LOOP

blocks.text: A nested loop puts one loop inside another. The outer counter controls rows; the inner counter controls columns. Reload the inner counter on every outer pass. If the inner body repeats P times and the outer loop repeats Q times with no early exit, the body runs P × Q times. Delay loops use nesting to stretch time without a huge count.

A delay loop is a loop whose only job is to consume a known time. The CPU does no useful work; it counts. The delay comes from the clock, not from the number of source lines. On the 8085, one T-state is one clock period. On the classic 8051, one machine cycle is 12 oscillator periods. Some syllabi call this a time delay loop.

blocks.where: T_total is the total clock periods, or T-states on the 8085; T_init is the setup time before the loop; N is the number of body executions; T_body is the body time without the conditional jump; T_taken is the jump time when taken; T_not is the jump time when not taken. For the 8085, delay = T_total / f_clk, where f_clk is the clock frequency.

blocks.text: On the 8051, DJNZ Rn,rel decrements Rn and branches if the result is not zero. It takes 2 machine cycles. At a 12 MHz crystal, one machine cycle is 1 µs, so one DJNZ takes 2 µs. Two hundred passes take about 400 µs, plus the setup instructions.
The last test fails, so the last conditional jump is not taken and is shorter. Count that final pass separately; do not multiply every pass by the taken time.

A look-up table is a block of constants in memory. The program computes an index, adds it to the table base, and reads the entry. The index is a byte offset, not the entry value. Tables replace long calculations with one memory read: seven-segment codes, sine samples, calibration points, square-root estimates.

On the 8085, LXI H,TABLE loads the base into HL. MVI E,index and MVI D,00H put a zero-extended index into DE. DAD D adds DE to HL. MOV A,M reads the selected entry. On the 8051, MOV DPTR,#TABLE sets the base, MOV A,#index sets the offset, and MOVC A,@A+DPTR reads code memory. On the 8086, put the base in BX and the index in AL, then execute XLAT; AL is replaced by the byte at DS:[BX+AL].

MOVC reads program memory, so an 8051 table is written with DB constants in code space. Use MOVX for a table in external data memory. XLAT uses AL as both index and result, so it can select at most 256 bytes. BX is not changed.

figure.caption: The loop loads FFH into C, decrements C, and jumps back until C becomes zero. The final test falls through to Exit, so the last conditional jump is not taken.

spec.title: Delay loop
spec.aria: The loop loads count FFH, decrements C, tests for zero, and jumps back until C becomes zero.

examples.question: An 8085 system runs at a 3 MHz clock. Find the delay produced by this loop: MVI C,FFH; LOOP: DCR C; JNZ LOOP. Use 7 T for MVI C,FFH, 4 T for DCR C, 10 T for JNZ when taken and 7 T when not taken.
steps: C = FFH = 255, so DCR C executes 255 times.
JNZ is taken on 254 passes and not taken on the final pass.
examples.answer: The loop delays about 1.19 ms, which is 1191.3 µs, from 3574 T-states at 3 MHz.
examples.check:
f_clk = 3e6
T_init = 7
T_body = 4
T_taken = 10
T_not = 7
N = 255
T = T_init + (N - 1) * (T_body + T_taken) + (T_body + T_not)
print(int(T))
delay_us = T / (f_clk / 1e6)
print(round(delay_us, 1))
print(round(delay_us / 1000, 2))

traps: Count T-states, not source lines. The three-line loop in the example runs thousands of T-states.
The last conditional jump is not taken. Using 10 T for every JNZ makes the delay too large.
On the 8051, one machine cycle is 12 oscillator periods. A 12 MHz crystal gives 1 µs machine cycles, not 0.083 µs.
DCR changes Z but not CY. Count-down loops test Z; do not test carry.
An 8085 table index goes into DE with D = 00H before DAD D. A non-zero D adds 256 × D to the address.
An 8051 MOVC table lives in code memory. MOVX reads external data memory, so it will not fetch a DB table in code space.

quiz.q: What operation does DJNZ Rn,rel perform?
quiz.a: It decrements register Rn, then branches to rel if the new value is not zero; otherwise it falls through.

quiz.q: Why is the final JNZ in a count-down delay loop timed as not taken?
quiz.a: The counter reaches zero on the last body pass, so the Z flag is set and the jump is not taken; that pass uses the shorter not-taken time.

quiz.q: An 8085 runs at 2 MHz. Find the delay for MVI C,64H; LOOP: DCR C; JNZ LOOP. Use 7 T, 4 T, 10 T taken, 7 T not taken.
quiz.a: 64H = 100, so 100 DCR passes and 99 taken JNZ. T = 7 + 99 × 14 + 11 = 1404 T. T-state = 0.5 µs, so delay = 702 µs.

quiz.q: Why does the inner counter of a nested delay loop need reloading on every outer pass?
quiz.a: Without reloading, the inner counter is 00H when the next outer pass begins. DCR then wraps it to FFH, so the inner loop runs 256 times instead of P; the delay is wrong. Reload the inner counter with P before every outer pass so each inner loop runs exactly P times.

quiz.q: An 8051 with a 12 MHz crystal runs DJNZ Rn,rel 200 times. Each DJNZ takes 2 machine cycles. Find the loop time, ignoring setup.
quiz.a: Machine cycle = 1 µs. One DJNZ = 2 µs. 200 × 2 µs = 400 µs.

quiz.q: In an 8085 table read, HL = 2100H and DE = 0005H. After DAD D, which address does MOV A,M read?
quiz.a: DAD D adds DE to HL: 2100H + 0005H = 2105H. MOV A,M reads the byte at 2105H.

quiz.q: Why must an 8085 byte index be zero-extended into DE before DAD D?
quiz.a: DAD D is a 16-bit add. The high byte must be 00H so the addition adds only the index, not an extra 256 × high-byte offset.

quiz.q: For 8086 XLAT, BX = 3000H and AL = 04H. What is in AL after XLAT, and what is BX?
quiz.a: AL becomes the byte at DS:3004H. BX stays 3000H.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern firmware usually replaces software delay loops with hardware timers, because a loop's timing changes when the clock, compiler or interrupt load changes. Cycle-accurate simulators and debug cycle counters verify timing without an oscilloscope. Look-up tables remain common for sine-wave PWM, gamma correction and sensor calibration, often stored in flash. Search next for 'DWT cycle counter', 'timer delay 8051' and 'lookup table sine PWM'.
